title: Batch formation heuristics for streaming chat completions (continuous batching + KV cache memory plan)
creator: Priya Sharma
description:
Goal: Design and implement batch-formation heuristics optimized for streaming chat completions that balance token-cost efficiency, latency SLOs, and GPU memory limits while maximizing KV-cache reuse. Scope covers scheduler heuristics, cache sharding rules, early-flush policies for streaming first tokens, and memory estimation models for mixed-sequence workloads.

Background: Continuous batching has improved throughput for non-streaming requests, but streaming chat workloads (low initial-latency requirement plus long-tail token generation) expose trade-offs: large batches increase token throughput but harm first-byte latency; naive batching breaks KV cache locality causing expensive cache repopulation and high GPU memory churn. We need heuristics that: (1) prioritize fast first-token delivery for streaming sessions, (2) opportunistically form larger background batches for steady long-token generation when SLOs permit, and (3) colocate requests to maximize KV cache hits and limit GPU memory fragmentation.

Proposed heuristics (high level):
- Two-tier batching pipeline: "fast-path" microbatches for streaming head tokens and "bulk-path" adaptive batches for continuing generation. Fast-path target size 1-4 requests or <= 64 tokens; bulk-path grows with observed seq-length distribution up to memory-bound batch size.
- Streaming-first flush: a configurable early-flush timeout (EFT) of 15-25ms that forces microbatch dispatch for any waiting streaming request to meet first-byte SLOs. EFT auto-tunes based on 95th percentile observed enqueue wait.
- Priority bucketing: requests carry a latency priority (streaming-high, interactive, batch-low). Scheduler assigns to buckets; cross-bucket batching allowed only when earliest enqueued in both buckets exceed EFT and combined batch fits memory budget.
- KV affinity grouping: prefer grouping requests that share conversation metadata (conversation_id, model, pinned prompt prefix). When affinity exists, keep them routed to same serving worker to reuse KV cache. Heuristic: prefer same-worker grouping if predicted KV reuse score >= 0.6 (score computed from prefix length overlap, recent KV hits, model variant).
- Prefix dedupe and compacted cache keys: detect identical or high-similarity prompt prefixes and dedupe by pointer to shared KV segments, reducing per-request cache memory.
- Dynamic memory budget estimator: per-request memory estimate = base_model_state + per-token_kv_size * seq_len + workspaces. Use recent telemetry to calibrate per-token_kv_size by model/quantization profile. Scheduler rejects batches predicted to exceed GPU memory safe threshold (configurable margin 8%).
- Background prefill windows: for long-running chats, allow background prefill of KV cache for predicted next tokens by reusing recently-seen KV segments (TTL-based) to reduce cache warm-up on worker handoffs. TTL default 5 minutes but tuned per-customer.
- Graceful fallback: when memory pressure prevents affinity grouping, fallback to cross-worker routing but mark sessions for slow-path adaptive throttling and later reclamation.
- Kernel selection hints: expose batch composition (max_seq, quant, dtypes) to runtime for selecting kernels that minimize temporary workspace memory (e.g., flash attention vs fallback kernels).

Experiments and metrics to collect:
- First-byte latency p50/p95/p99 for streaming heads pre/post heuristic change. Target p50 <= 20ms for fast-path, p95 <= 50ms for streaming-first.
- Tokens/sec and GPU utilization change for mixed traffic. Goal: >=10% throughput gain for bulk-path without regressing streaming p95.
- KV cache hit-rate and average KV-cache population churn per worker. Aim to reduce churn by >=20% for affinity-grouped sessions.
- Memory OOM/eviction events and margin headroom distribution.

Implementation plan (milestones):
1) Simulation harness (2w): build offline simulator that replays production traces with streaming flags, conversation-affinity markers, and seq-length distributions. Output is predicted batch sizes, memory usage, and latency trade-offs.
2) Scheduler prototype (2w): implement two-tier queue with EFT, priority bucketing, and simple KV affinity score. Add feature flags for rollout.
3) Memory estimator and kernel hinting (1w): integrate estimator into scheduler and surface batch composition to runtime.
4) Canary rollout (1w): deterministic subset of traffic + A/B tests measuring first-byte latency and throughput.
5) Full rollout + tuning (2w).

Risks and mitigations:
- Risk: Over-clustering by affinity may cause hot-worker memory pressure. Mitigation: global hot-spot detector triggers split routing and preemptive TTL shrinkage.
- Risk: EFT too aggressive reduces throughput. Mitigation: EFT auto-tune and allow per-customer overrides.
- Risk: KV dedupe complexity introduces bugs in cache invalidation. Mitigation: start with read-only dedupe (pointer sharing) and add invalidation hooks in next phase.

Acceptance criteria:
- Simulator demonstrates net latency/throughput win on 3 recent production traces.
- Canary meets first-byte SLOs and reduces KV churn by >= 15% in canary cohort.
- No increase in OOM rate beyond baseline (target <= baseline + 1%).

Implementation notes for assignee:
- Start by instrumenting current enqueue wait histograms and per-request metadata exposure (conversation_id, streaming flag, pinned_model). We'll need these in trace to compute affinity scores.
- Keep scheduling logic behind a feature flag with experiment metadata to allow rollback.
- Add metrics: scheduler.batch_type, scheduler.batch_composition, scheduler.predicted_mem, kv.affinity_score, kv.reuse_hit
